query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: For noble-metal high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles that nominally favour the face-centred-cubic (fcc) solid-solution state, the decisive control parameter for whether a single-phase fcc particle forms is the maximum processing temperature (T_peak) reached relative to the weighted‐average equilibrium melting point of the alloy (T_m,alloy). When T_peak ≥ 0.9 T_m,alloy, atomic diffusion during the short high-T dwell produces near-equilibrium chemical mixing; upon rapid quench the high configurational entropy (ΔS_conf) stabilises a single-phase fcc solid solution. If T_peak ≤ 0.8 T_m,alloy the atoms never reach the mobility required to overcome element-specific reduction/onset temperatures and surface-segregation energies, so reduction proceeds sequentially, leading to compositional inhomogeneity, phase separation or stacking-fault–rich (hcp-like or multiply-twinned) particles. Thus, crystal-structure selection (single-phase fcc vs mixed/hcp/twinned) is governed by the competition between (i) high-temperature entropy-driven bulk mixing and (ii) low-temperature, surface/kinetic segregation, with the crossover set by T_peak/T_m,alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic precursor mixture of ≥6 noble metals that individually adopt fcc lattices at ambient pressure (e.g. Ag-Au-Pd-Pt-Ir-Cu) in solution or supported on inert oxide, before thermal processing; no long-range order and no pre-formed nuclei.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the thermal shock peak temperature (T_peak) while keeping composition, atmosphere, pressure, ramp rate (>10^4 K s⁻¹), and quench rate constant; compare samples processed at T_peak values spanning 0.7–1.1 T_m,alloy.
generation.conditions: Inert (Ar or N₂) atmosphere, pressure ≈1 bar, heating ramp ≥10^4 K s⁻¹, dwell <1 s, quench to <400 K in <10 ms; particle size 5–20 nm; total metal loading ≤10 wt %.
generation.structural_mediator: Extent of atomic interdiffusion during the high-T dwell as quantified by nearest-neighbour chemical mixing entropy (or Warren–Cowley parameters) measured ex situ.
generation.mechanism: At T_peak ≥ 0.9 T_m,alloy atoms are sufficiently mobile that multi-body exchange (vacancy and surface diffusion) randomises element distribution, lowering the configurational free energy (ΔG = ΔH_mix – TΔS_conf). Rapid quenching freezes this homogeneous state as a metastable fcc solid solution. Below ≈0.8 T_m,alloy limited diffusion confines atoms to nuclei that form sequentially according to individual reduction potentials; concomitant surface energy minimisation drives Ag/Au enrichment at the surface and Pt/Ir enrichment inside, producing chemical segregation, stacking faults, and hcp or multiply-twinned domains.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with a baseline sample processed at T_peak ≈ 1.0 T_m,alloy that shows a single-phase fcc pattern (sharp fcc XRD peaks, uniform STEM–EDS maps), samples treated at T_peak ≤ 0.8 T_m,alloy will exhibit: (1) broadened or split diffraction peaks indicative of hcp or bimetallic phases, (2) core–shell or patchy elemental segregation in STEM–EDS, and (3) higher onset temperature for thermogravimetric decomposition due to residual precursors. Intermediate T_peak (0.8–0.9 T_m,alloy) will give mixed signatures.
generation.baseline: Single-phase, chemically homogeneous fcc HEA nanoparticles prepared at T_peak ≈ 1.0 T_m,alloy under the same ramp/quench rates.
generation.boundary: Applies to equiatomic or near-equiatomic (>5 elements) noble-metal sets in which each constituent is fcc in bulk and whose weighted T_m,alloy lies between 1250 K and 1800 K. Does not necessarily extend to systems containing non-fcc solutes (e.g. Re, Ru) or to particle sizes >30 nm (where surface effects are reduced) or <2 nm (where discrete shell closings dominate).
generation.uncertainty: Exact numerical threshold (0.9 versus 0.85 T_m,alloy) may shift with ramp rate and particle size; role of support interactions is not included; lack of direct data on nanoscale T_m,alloy may introduce ±5 % error.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a single batch of equiatomic AgAuPdPtIrCu nanoparticles on carbon paper. Divide into five aliquots, subject each to identical 10^4 K s⁻¹ ramps but distinct T_peak values: 0.75, 0.82, 0.90, 0.97 and 1.05 T_m,alloy. Quench identically. Characterise crystal structure by synchrotron XRD and local chemical order by atomic-resolution STEM-EDS and EXAFS.
measurements: Phase fractions from Rietveld refinement of XRD
Stacking fault probability from whole-pattern fitting
Elemental distribution maps and line scans
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If a single-phase, chemically homogeneous fcc structure is obtained for all samples including those processed at T_peak ≤ 0.8 T_m,alloy, OR if any sample processed at T_peak ≥ 0.95 T_m,alloy consistently shows multi-phase segregation or dominant hcp/twinned structures, the hypothesis is falsified.
